messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Theoretic question about HMC
parts:
Let’s review the basics of HMC.  We have our target distribution, pi(q) = exp(-V(q)),
and the conditional distribution of the momenta, pi(p|q) = exp(-T(q, p)).  The HMC
transition is then (i) sample the momenta, p ~ pi(p|q) (ii) evolve using Hamiltonian flow,
(q, p) -> \phi_{t} (q, p) (iii) marginalize the momenta, (q, p) -> q.  Each step in the
operation preserves pi(q) and so the entire transition preserves pi(q) and yields a
desired sample.  Note that T(q, p) can be almost anything and there is no Metropolis 
correction here.

Now in practice we can’t do (ii) exactly and we have to approximate the flow with
a symplectic integrator.  This introduces error and pi(q) is no longer preserved
exactly.  Typically we fix this by treating the approximate flow as a proposal and
add a Metropolis correction, but this requires that the flow be reversible which
it is not.  To make the flow reversible we can do a few things — we can sample
the integration time from any distribution symmetric around zero or, if the
kinetic energy is symmetric with respect to p, we can add a momentum flip
at the end of the flow, (q, p) -> (q, -p).  Outside of NUTS people typically consider
a fixed integration time which leaves only the second option, hence the importance 
of the symmetry of the kinetic energy.

What you’ve proposed is to sample from a distribution pi(p|q) = exp(-L(q, p))
that is not related to the kinetic energy.  Immediately this will cause a problem
because (i) will preserve only exp(-L) while (ii) preserves only exp(-T) and
the combined transition no longer has a stationary distribution.  So the exact
HMC algorithm doesn’t work.  We can still try to use this as a Metropolis-Hastings
proposal (although a poorly performing one) if we can make it reversible.
How we make it reversible depends on the choice of L(q, p), but it general
it will not be an easy problem.

Note that choosing a kinetic energy is a somewhat subtle problem.  Nominally
there are no constraints on T(q, p) which is usually a really bad sign — the
more the math constrains our options the less tuning we have to do and the
more robust the algorithm will be.  One way to introduce constraints is to
introduce more structure, such as a metric.  It turns out that a metric gives
a canonical family of kinetic energies with nice properties, and every member
of that family is symmetric because of the symmetry of the metric.  So 
asymmetric kinetic energies are not only awkward to use they’re actually
really hard to motivate in the first place.

For all the gory details see http://arxiv.org/abs/1410.5110.

( Statement 2) But if we are approximating the Hamilton’s equations by discretizing time (using leapfrog) then the acceptance probability [from <tblatex-22.png> to <tblatex-21.png>] won't be simply <tblatex-18.png>

We would have to find <tblatex-17.png> for which <tblatex-16.png> will be the proposal values if we start from <tblatex-15.png>

And, in this case, the acceptance probability will be: <tblatex-23.png>

Are both  statements correct? If so, it seems that it's pretty difficult to find the value of <tblatex-17.png>...

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Theoretic question about HMC
parts:
You can use latex with $latex ...$ in WordPress.

When I was thinking about detailed balance the other day I made
up two examples which I found super helpful for understanding mixing.

I'm not sure why I haven't seen this before or maybe I have and just
didn't remember.

Consider a Markov chain with transition probabilities:

A -> A : 0.4 B -> A : 0.4
A -> B : 0.6 B -> B : 0.6

It's easy to see with this example that the stationary distribution
for a chain y drawn this way has

Pr[y[t] = A] = 0.4
Pr[y[t] = B] = 0.6

In fact, this Markov chain is really just a sequence of independent
draws because the chance of being in A at time t+1 doesn't depend on
which state you're in at time t.

Contrast that with transition probabilities:

A -> A : 0.9 B -> A : 1/15
A -> B : 0.1 B -> B : 14/15

This produces chains with the the same stationary distribution, but
it doesn't mix as well due to the autocorrelation.

The detailed balance condition is that the probability of being in
state A and moving to B is the same as being in B and moving to A.

Pr[A] * Pr[A -> B] = Pr[B] * Pr[A -> B]

You can verify it for the above chains.

You can think of continuous versions of MCMC the same way --- you
just partition the space into two pieces, A and B, and look at probabilities
of transitioning between them (or generalize to more states). It makes
much more sense (to me at least) than thinking about densities --- for
instance, it makes the Goodman and Weare ensemble sampler clearer as to
why it needs to do the Jacobian adjustment it does.

This is going on a slide or two for our upcoming class where I believe
I'm on the hook to do a day of Bayes and MCMC.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Theoretic question about HMC
parts:
The general state space version of Metropolis-Hastings works
in a similar way.  Basically, you double your target space,
\Omega -> \Omega \times \Omega, and then the 
Metropolis-Hastings proposal is just switching the the states
in the two components of the product space (formally, the
acceptance probability is the Radon-Nikodym derivative
of the transition from component one into component two
with respect to the transition from component two into
component one).

Anyways, the point is that detailed balance follows immediately
from the permutation-like construction of the general
Metropolis-Hastings algorithm.  In fact, most Markov transitions
can be framed in this way.
